01.actor: Rav Anan bar Taḥalifa (and Rav Ashi)
01.event: Each recalls standing as waiter before a master who was served a fragrant dish.
01.turn: The waiter craved the food and would have been endangered had he not been given some.
01.outcome: The master gave him a share; the tellers draw a rule that aromatic or sharp foods must be shared.
01.summary: Rav Anan bar Taḥalifa says he once stood before Mar Shmuel as a dish of mushrooms was brought, and he would have been endangered by craving had Shmuel not given him some. Rav Ashi tells a similar story about turnip slices in vinegar served to Rav Kahana. These are brief testimonies offered as evidence for a rule about sharing strongly flavored food.
01.missing: Little detail of the scenes; the anecdotes serve a legal point.

02.event: While sitting before Rabbi Yannai he declared that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda.
02.turn: Rabbi Yannai rejected the ruling as wrong.
02.outcome: Yannai told him to go outside and recite his verses, since the halakha is not like Rabbi Yehuda.
02.summary: Rabbi Ḥanina Kara, a Bible reciter, sat before Rabbi Yannai and stated that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yannai sharply told him to go outside and recite his verses there, because the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.

03.event: Rava taught that one may scatter straw on a rain-damaged courtyard on Shabbat, and Rav Pappa objected from a baraita.
03.outcome: He had a spokesman publicly announce that his earlier statement was a mistake and gave the correct rule.
03.summary: Rava taught that on Shabbat one may spread straw on a courtyard ruined by rain. Rav Pappa challenged him with a baraita requiring a different manner of scattering. Rava then appointed a spokesman and publicly announced that his earlier statement was his mistake, and gave the rule as taught in Rabbi Eliezer's name.

04.actor: A man who sold land to Rav Pappa, and Rav Pappa
04.event: A man sold land to Rav Pappa to raise money for oxen.
04.turn: He ended up not needing the money and regretted the sale.
04.outcome: Rav Pappa returned the land, which the Gemara says was beyond the letter of the law.
04.summary: A man sold land to Rav Pappa because he needed cash to buy oxen. In the end he did not need the money, and Rav Pappa gave the land back to him. The Gemara dismisses this as proof, since Rav Pappa acted beyond the strict letter of the law.

05.missing: The passage is a halakhic and exegetical discussion of how girls' ripeness was known, not a narrative of events.

06.missing: The passage reconstructs a hypothetical legal case about witnesses and a challenge, with no actual event.

07.actor: A person who let witnesses trace their names on non-divorce documents, and Rav Kahana
07.event: A person allowed witnesses to trace their names on other documents, not bills of divorce.
07.turn: This went beyond the leniency allowed only for divorce bills.
07.summary: The leniency of having witnesses trace names written in saliva applies only to bills of divorce. One person nevertheless did this for other documents, and Rav Kahana had him flogged for it.
07.missing: Identity of the person and details of the incident.

08.event: A man declared his property should go to Toviya and then died.
08.turn: Toviya came to claim it, raising doubt whether another Toviya was meant.
08.outcome: Rabbi Yoḥanan said Toviya has come, so the property goes to him.
08.summary: A man told those around him that his property should go to Toviya, and then he died. Toviya came to claim it, and Rabbi Yoḥanan ruled that Toviya had indeed come, so there was no need to worry about another Toviya.

09.event: Rav Kahana held the beer of an orphan, Rav Mesharshiyya, and delayed selling it until the Festival.
09.turn: The beer might sour a little in the wait.
09.outcome: He explained it would fetch cash at a better price at the Festival.
09.summary: Rav Kahana was guardian of beer belonging to an orphan, Rav Mesharshiyya bar Ḥilkai. He held off selling it until the Festival, saying that although it might spoil a little, it would bring in real money then.

10.actor: A man pining for a woman, as told by Ilfa
10.event: A man in Eretz Yisrael, suffering over a woman, wanted to leave the land.
10.turn: He heard the teaching about the great significance of living in Eretz Yisrael.
10.outcome: He stayed and suffered there until the day he died.
10.summary: Rabba's brothers wrote to him in Babylonia relaying Ilfa's story of a man who longed for a certain woman and wanted to leave Eretz Yisrael. When he heard the teaching about the importance of staying there, he remained and suffered until he died. The rest of the letter is advice urging Rabba to come.
10.missing: Who the man and woman were and why leaving was connected to her; the rest of the passage is advice, not story.

11.event: He wished to give away much movable property as a gift but could only do so by transfer through land.
11.turn: He bought a small plot near Jerusalem and declared the gift together with the land.
11.outcome: He died and the Sages upheld his words.
11.summary: A man from Madon in Jerusalem had much movable property and wanted to give it away. The Sages told him it could only be transferred together with land, so he bought a plot near Jerusalem and gave a portion of it to someone along with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels. He died, and the Sages upheld his words.

12.actor: Rava and a woman whose husband died in a famine
12.event: A woman came before Rava and testified that her husband died in a famine.
12.turn: Rava cross-examined her and she admitted he could not have survived on what she left, showing she did not see him die.
12.outcome: Rava concluded famine is like war and retracted his earlier view.
12.summary: Rava first thought famine differs from war for a wife's testimony of death. A woman then came and said her husband died in famine; Rava asked whether he could have survived on the little flour she left him, and she answered that he could not. Seeing she had not witnessed his death, Rava changed his ruling to treat famine like war.

13.event: Ravina had Rav Ashi's daughter collect her one-tenth share from two estates.
13.turn: From one son he gave intermediate land without oath, and from an orphan inferior land with oath.
13.outcome: This is taken as proof she was treated as creditor of the sons.
13.summary: Ravina arranged for Rav Ashi's daughter to collect her share from the estate: intermediate-quality land without an oath from Mar, and inferior-quality land with an oath from an orphan grandson. The Gemara reads this as evidence about whose creditor she was. It is a precedent report more than a story.
13.missing: No real narrative arc; the account serves as legal proof.
